cim: The Juice Is Worth the (Mechanical) Squeeze
cim_eredeti: The Juice Is Worth the (Mechanical) Squeeze
szoveg_eredeti:
We’re inundated with articles telling us that our need for electricity will soon outstrip our current means of production. Hopeful eyes look to small modular reactors (SMRs). But even under expedited permitting and construction those are 5 – 10 years away. Gas turbines are efficient, economical, fast to deploy and relatively clean. But the turbine manufacturers have an order backlog that runs into years. Solar and wind power cannot fill the gap in the short term.

So then, do we consign ourselves to be a second rate technological player while waiting for means of electricity production to catch up with consumption? No. In prior periods of “energy crisis” – whether it was the notion that the US had run out of natural gas, or that “Peak Oil” had occurred, scientific advancements have shown up in time. Chief among these advancements were horizontal fracturing (“fracking”) and space age advancements in geological and geophysical imaging. The “next gen” in energy developments lies in fission and fusion nuclear power. But until SMRs come online and their larger siblings come out of hibernation, a much older technology is here to fill the gap.

Using today’s example, as I write this, Anthropic floated its initial public offering, imputing a $2 trillion market capitalization. Clearly, investors are betting on a bright future for artificial intelligence, meaning an equally bright future (no pun intended) for electricity.

Anthropic did not bet blindly on future energy development. Rather it, and many others needing on demand, real-time electricity, are investing in their own captive power plants, sited next to the facilities they will power. These plants will not need to draw power from the existing power grid, and in some communities, are promised to feed power, free of charge, into the power grid, benefiting local communities.

As our friend Robert Bryce wrote in his Substack article, Anthropic’s preferred strategy is renting generation facilities from third parties. But it recently announced a $3.4B Gas Generator deal to power its AI data centers. It is an acquisition of already placed orders for: heavy‑duty gas‑fired Otto cycle generators manufactured by Caterpillar, each capable of up to 1.7 GW output; engineering and construction services to install the equipment at Anthropic’s facilities; and delivery expected within the next two years, avoiding a six‑year U.S. waitlist for new large turbines. According to TechCrunch, quoting the Financial Times, Reuters, and CNBC, the agreement was reached in late September 2026 to take over orders placed by OnePwr, a Texas company, two years ago. OnePwr was apparently unable to find financing, so flipped its order book to Anthropic. However, Anthropic is not acquiringOnePWR or its employees.

I mentioned the use of old technology above. As Bryce reminds us, these heavy duty gas engines (manufactured by Caterpillar, Wartsilla (a Finnish engine manufacturer), Bergen Engines and Huyndai among others) are “Otto cycle” engines, a technology named after the first person to successfully build a 4 stroke engine, in the late 1800’s. Today, according to one of the manufacturer’s websites, these engines can achieve “combined cycle” efficiency of approximately 54 %. That’s roughly 90% of the efficiency of modern turbines, but at less cost. These will provide the bridge to future, more permanent power solutions.
